hops.afterHeading: Count each sense by its reliability
hops.title: Two beeps can make one flash look like two
hops.text: It is tempting to think vision always overrules other senses. For location, a sharp visual cue usually wins, as Alais and Burr found. Counting quick events is different. Ladan Shams, Yukiyasu Kamitani and Shinsuke Shimojo paired one flash with two quick beeps, and volunteers often reported two flashes. In a separate timing experiment, one beep started with the flash; the illusion weakened near 70-millisecond offsets yet remained measurable at 115 milliseconds. Shams, Wei Ji Ma and Ulrik Beierholm later compared sound-only and flash-only trials: people counted beeps more reliably than flashes, and combined reports fit a Bayesian model using single-sense reliability and nonuniform flash-beep priors.

sources.citation: Alais D, Burr D (2004). The ventriloquist effect results from near-optimal bimodal integration. Current Biology 14(3):257-262.
Shams L, Kamitani Y, Shimojo S (2002). Visual illusion induced by sound. Cognitive Brain Research 14(1):147-152.
Shams L, Ma WJ, Beierholm U (2005). Sound-induced flash illusion as an optimal percept. NeuroReport 16(17):1923-1927.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A student seen from behind holds up two fingers at a monitor showing one white circle between two small speakers.
image.caption: One flash with two quick beeps often looks like two flashes, fitting a Bayesian model of reliability and nonuniform priors.

hops.afterHeading: A fish that learns to cancel its own pulse
hops.title: A singing cricket turns down its own song
hops.text: A male field cricket faces the electric fish's problem and solves it differently. His ears sit on his forelegs, fully exposed to his own loud song. James Poulet and Berthold Hedwig recorded inside singing crickets, Gryllus bimaculatus. In phase with each sound pulse of every chirp, a signal from the singing circuit weakens transmission at the terminals of the auditory nerve fibers and inhibits an identified auditory interneuron, even in an isolated nervous system singing silently. In 2006 they traced both effects to one identified type of corollary-discharge interneuron. The timed inhibition dampens his response to his own song and helps him stay sensitive to quieter sounds between chirps.

sources.citation: Poulet JFA, Hedwig B (2002). A corollary discharge maintains auditory sensitivity during sound production. Nature 418:872-876.
Poulet JFA, Hedwig B (2006). The cellular basis of a corollary discharge. Science 311:518-522.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A dark field cricket on a blade of grass sings with raised wings while a small pale moth hovers nearby.
image.caption: Brief inhibition dampens a cricket's neural response to its own song, preserving auditory sensitivity to quieter sounds between chirps.

hops.afterHeading: Mouse cortex: a movement signal and a mismatch signal
hops.title: The SpeechJammer and the delayed voice
hops.text: In 2012 Kazutaka Kurihara and Koji Tsukada won the Ig Nobel Prize in Acoustics for the SpeechJammer, a gadget meant to quiet people who hog a meeting. A direction-sensitive microphone and speaker play the talker's own words back a few hundred milliseconds late. In a five-person preliminary study, the authors observed the device disrupting speech while a person was talking. Earlier, Yasuki Hashimoto and Kuniyoshi Sakai delayed volunteers' voices by 200 milliseconds in a scanner. Auditory areas in the temporal lobe on both sides were more active than with real-time feedback, especially in people who lost more fluency. The authors linked that activity to monitoring one's own speech.

sources.citation: Kurihara K, Tsukada K (2012). SpeechJammer: a system utilizing artificial speech disturbance with delayed auditory feedback. arXiv:1202.6106.
Improbable Research. Ig Nobel Prize winners (2012 Acoustics Prize).
Hashimoto Y, Sakai KL (2003). Brain activations during conscious self-monitoring of speech production with delayed auditory feedback: an fMRI study. Human Brain Mapping 20(1):22-28.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A handheld directional microphone and speaker prototype rests on a conference table beside a coffee mug and blank cards.
image.caption: Hearing your own voice a fraction of a second late can make fluent speech falter.
